# TypeScript Architecture & Type Systems Mastery Track

Welcome to the TypeScript Architecture & Type Systems Mastery Track materialized with Trak.

## Curriculum Structure

00 — Setup, Toolchain & First Program
01 — Primitive Types & Type Annotations
02 — Literal Types & Union Types
03 — Objects, Type Aliases & Interfaces
04 — Arrays, Tuples & Readonly
05 — Generics & Type Parameters
06 — Generic Constraints & Keyof
07 — Type Narrowing & Discriminated Unions
08 — Utility Types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record
09 — Conditional Types & Infer
10 — Asynchronous TypeScript & Result Pattern
11 — Mapped Types & Key Remapping
12 — Template Literal Types
13 — Classes & Access Modifiers
14 — Abstract Classes & Polymorphism
15 — Function Overloads & Signatures
16 — Advanced Type Guards & Predicates
17 — Branded & Nominal Types
18 — Utility Types: Exclude, Extract, ReturnType
19 — Modules & Type-Only Imports

## Verification Commands

```bash
# Verify current pending exercise:
trak verify

# Verify specific module:
trak verify 01

# Verify all modules:
trak verify --all
```

# 00 — Setup, Toolchain & First Program

## What is this?
Welcome to TypeScript! TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript by adding static type definitions. You do not need to solve complex type puzzles or pass automated tests in this introductory module. You will learn how TypeScript code runs, how types work at compile time, and how to execute your first TypeScript file.

## Why does TypeScript have it?
- JavaScript is dynamically typed, meaning type errors (such as calling a method that does not exist or passing `undefined` to a function) are only discovered when users trigger them in production.
- TypeScript introduces a compile-time static type checker that catches bugs while you write code in your editor.
- At runtime, TypeScript types are completely erased (stripped away). The JavaScript engine (V8 / Node.js) executes the clean underlying JavaScript with zero runtime performance overhead.

## The Minimal Anatomy of a TypeScript Program
Take a look at `index.ts` in this directory:

```typescript
const greeting: string = "Hello, TypeScript!";
console.log(greeting);
```

Let us break down each part:
1. `const greeting`: Declares an immutable variable identifier.
2. `: string`: A static type annotation. Informs the TypeScript compiler that `greeting` must always be a string. If you attempt to assign a number to it, the compiler will refuse to build.
3. `"Hello, TypeScript!"`: The string value.
4. `console.log(...)`: Standard output printing to terminal.

## How to Run Your First Program
Open your terminal in this directory and execute:

### 1. Run the script directly with Node
Modern Node.js executes TypeScript natively by stripping type annotations:
```bash
node index.ts
```
You will see:
```text
Hello, TypeScript!
```

### 2. Type-check your project with the TypeScript compiler
If you have `tsc` installed globally or via npm:
```bash
npx tsc --noEmit
```
This runs the full TypeScript type checker across your workspace without generating output files, confirming that your types are 100% valid.

## Common Mistakes
1. Expecting types to exist at runtime: Writing `if (typeof x === "MyInterface")` will fail because TypeScript interfaces and type aliases do not exist in the compiled JavaScript runtime.
2. Confusing TypeScript with a separate runtime: Node.js or the browser executes JavaScript; TypeScript is the author-time type system that ensures safety before runtime.

## What to Practice
1. Open `index.ts`.
2. Run `node index.ts` in your terminal to verify output.
3. Change the message to `"Hello, Trak!"` or your name, save, and run `node index.ts` again.
4. Run `trak verify 00` or `trak done 00` to mark this setup complete and proceed to Module 01!

# 09 — Conditional Types & Infer

## What is this?
Conditional types select one of two possible types based on a condition expressed as a type relationship test: `T extends U ? X : Y`. The `infer` keyword allows you to declare a type variable within the condition to extract (unpack) inner types dynamically.

## Why does TypeScript have it?
- Powers advanced type transformations like unpacking Promise results (`Awaited<T>`), extracting array item types, or reading function return types (`ReturnType<T>`).

## Basic Syntax
```typescript
// If T is an array, extract item type, else return T
type Flatten<T> = T extends (infer Item)[] ? Item : T;

type StringItem = Flatten<string[]>; // string
type SingleNumber = Flatten<number>; // number

// Unpack Promise
type UnwrapPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T;
```

## How it Behaves
1. Distributive Conditional Types: When the checked type is a bare type parameter and a union is passed, the condition distributes across the union:
   ```typescript
   type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
   type Res = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]
   ```
2. `infer`: Introduces a new generic type variable that is deduced by pattern matching against the structure of `T`.

## Common Mistakes
1. Trying to use `infer` outside of an `extends` conditional clause: `infer` can only be placed inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type.
2. Forgetting that unions distribute: If distribution is undesired, wrap both sides in square brackets: `[T] extends [any] ? ...`.

## Small Practical Example
```typescript
type ElementType<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] as const;
type Color = ElementType<typeof colors>; // "red" | "green" | "blue"
```

## What to Practice
Implement in `exercise.ts`:
1. Define type `UnpackPromise<T>`: If `T extends Promise<infer U>`, returns `U`, otherwise returns `T`.
2. Define type `FirstArgument<T>`: If `T extends (first: infer A, ...rest: any[]) => any`, returns `A`, otherwise returns `never`.
3. `unwrapValue<T>(val: T): T extends Promise<infer R> ? Promise<R> : T`:
   - If `val` is a Promise, returns the promise. Otherwise returns `val`.

## Progressive Hints
- Hint 1: `type UnpackPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;`
- Hint 2: `type FirstArgument<T> = T extends (first: infer A, ...args: any[]) => any ? A : never;`

## Reference Solution

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal reference solution</summary>

```typescript
export type UnpackPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;

export type FirstArgument<T> = T extends (first: infer A, ...args: any[]) => any ? A : never;

export function unwrapValue<T>(val: T): T extends Promise<infer R> ? Promise<R> : T {
    return val as any;
}
```
</details>
